extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially Kantian philosophy) interested in teleology and the Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing Kant's distinctions and evaluative principles for judging purposiveness in nature (internal vs external purposiveness, final purposes, the role of man, and the limits of physico-theology). Focused on conceptual criteria for when teleological explanation is appropriate and what it can and cannot justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: External purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: By external purposiveness I mean that by which one thing of nature serves another as means to a purpose. Things which have no internal purposiveness (e.g. earth, air, water) may at the same time be very purposive externally, i.e. in relation to other beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External purposiveness requires that the thing judged as a means stand in relation to organised beings (natural purposes); examples: water, air, and earth can be means to organised beings but cannot be regarded as means to mountains. External purposiveness differs from internal purposiveness because it does not imply the object is itself a purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal purposiveness is bound up with the possibility of an object irrespective of its actuality being itself a purpose; we can ask of an organised being: 'What is it for?' and represent its causality according to purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal purposiveness implies a causality according to final causes and an Idea at its ground; it is the condition under which we represent an active faculty (e.g., formative impulse) as directed by design. Only organised beings admit of internal purposive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection of external and internal purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is only one external purposiveness which is connected with the internal purposiveness of organisation, and yet serves in the external relation of a means to a purpose, without the question necessarily arising as to what end this being so organised must have existed for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the organisation of both sexes in their mutual relation for propagation — here we can ask 'why must such a pair exist?' because the pair constitutes an organising whole, though not an organised whole in a single body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final purpose vs means (final purpose criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the existence of a natural being can either be in itself (a final purpose) or external to it in another natural being (purposive as a means). A final purpose needs no other as condition of its possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must distinguish whether an object's purposiveness is self-contained (final) or only as a means. Kant argues that, when surveyed, nature contains no being that can claim to be the final purpose of creation (in the empirical world).

rubrics_metrics.name: Man as candidate for ultimate purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is the only being on earth who can form a concept of purposes and who can by his Reason make out of an aggregate of purposively formed things a system of purposes; thus man can be judged as the ultimate purpose of nature here on earth (for reflective judgement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a reflective judgement: insofar as man can set arbitrary purposes by reason, he can be conceived as the ultimate purpose, but only under the condition that he has an Understanding and a Will able to posit ends independently of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness cannot be the final purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of happiness is an Idea of a state man wishes to make adequate to empirical conditions; it is vacillating and cannot serve as an unconditioned final purpose in an earthly system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is empirical, variable, and not something nature could reliably realize as an unconditioned final purpose because human dispositions, destructive forces, and internal contradictions prevent its universal attainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as the ultimate purpose of nature (formal condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture — the production of the aptitude of a rational being for arbitrary purposes in general (consequently in his freedom) — is the only natural end adequate to be ascribed to nature in respect of the human race; it is the formal subjective condition for a final purpose outside nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture is not the matter of earthly purposes but the formal capacity to set purposes; thus nature's role is to prepare humans for freedom and moral finality by developing the aptitude for purposiveness (culture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture of skill (technical cultivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The culture of skill is the chief subjective condition of aptitude for furthering one’s purposes in general; it develops natural capacities through division of labor, arts, science, and luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skill develops via inequality and specialised labor; it fosters cultural achievements but is insufficient alone to cultivate the will (moral determination) — it contributes to aptitude but not to moral finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture of training (discipline of the will)
rubrics_metrics.description: The culture of training (discipline) is negative and consists in the freeing of the will from the despotism of desires; it is necessary for furthering the will in the determination and choice of purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline enables autonomy of the will by restraining sensuous inclinations; both skill and discipline are needed for full culture, but discipline is essential for moral self-legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socio-political arrangement for cultural development
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal condition under which nature can attain its final design (development of natural capacities) is an arrangement of men’s relations in which lawful authority in a whole (a civil community) restrains abuse of conflicting freedoms; ideally a cosmopolitan whole would be requisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A civil community permits maximum development of capacities; absence of a cosmopolitan system leads to war, ambition, and division, which impede the harmonious development of culture. Kant even suggests war may serve as a hidden means to political unity via law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of mechanical and teleological explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest effort to explain organic forms mechanically is permitted and invited by Reason, yet we (by our constitution of understanding) cannot conceive certain organised beings except according to final causes; both ways of representing the possibility of nature may be compatible via a supersensible principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical explanations concern production under particular laws; teleological explanations are principles of reflective judgement that do not determine origin but guide how we must represent organised beings. The two are not mutually exclusive in our representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective judgement vs determinant judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological and mechanical methods are merely principles of the reflective Judgement in respect of nature as it produces forms according to particular laws (for the systematic connexion of which we have no key); they do not determine the origin of these beings in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflective judgement seeks systematic unity and employs final-purpose representations when determinative principles fail; determinant judgement applies laws to given purposes/objects. Teleology functions as a regulative, not constitutive, principle regarding origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of Physico-theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Physico-theology is the endeavour of Reason to infer the Supreme Cause of nature and its properties from the purposes of nature (empirically known); it can justify the concept of an intelligent World Cause as a subjective concept but cannot disclose a final purpose of creation or determine the Supreme Cause's properties beyond empirical effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physico-theology supplies insight into how natural arrangements suggest design and can prompt theological ideas, but empirical data cannot yield a determinate concept of a Supreme Being adequate for theology; theoretical use of Reason lacks grounds to add the necessary supplements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between physico-theology and moral (ethico-) theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Physico-theology infers the Supreme Cause from purposes of nature (empirical); moral theology (ethico-theology) infers it from the moral purpose of rational beings (a priori). The former naturally precedes the latter, but cannot by itself found a theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the practical (moral) use of Reason can provide an a priori Idea prompting supplementation of the limited theoretical concept derived from nature; moral theology addresses final purpose in a way physico-theology cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives explaining purposiveness (mechanism, idealism, multiple intelligences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three alternatives to a single intelligent Designer: (1) explain Teleology as deception and adopt mere mechanism; (2) adopt Idealism of final causes (unity of substance leading to apparent purposiveness) leading toward Pantheism/Spinozism; (3) posit many intelligent original beings or a single one but acknowledge empirical data cannot determine unity or properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each alternative has trade-offs: pure mechanism dissolves purposiveness, idealism explains purposiveness as inherence rather than design, and empirical support cannot decide between multiple designers or one with full attributes; theoretical Reason alone cannot justify adding perfection to the empirical concept of a World Cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of a priori practical Reason to justify theological attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: To extend the limited empirical concept of an original Understanding into the Idea of an Allwise, Infinite Being (Deity) requires a use of Reason that is not theoretical but practical (a priori); theoretical investigation of nature cannot legitimately ascribe omniscience or omnipotence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that adding attributes to the empirical concept (to reach a useful theology) presupposes the a priori moral Idea of a Supreme Being; without such practical grounds, theoretical reasoning lacks justification to posit divine perfections.
